learning_outcomes.description: Communicate effectively on contemporary conceptual and methodological knowledge in anthropology and its relevance to other disciplines and the world.
Apply advanced skills in critically reviewing anthropological literature, analysing case studies, and considering the positionality of researchers.
Identify an area or areas of anthropological knowledge to which you seek to contribute in future work or study.

assessments.task_description:
Critical questions: summarise a key point from the literature and write a critical/reflexive question that arises from that summary: Complete only 4 of 7 available = 40%

Students will be provided with a blank one-page worksheet at the end of class: In 30 minutes, write a 1-2 sentence summary of the weekly reading: 2 authors’ arguments (from the three listed for the week) + raise a conceptual question or theoretical reflection on the work. May rely on dot point notes taken during class/ seminar discussion, or notes prepared prior to the class. No online use, no AI use during writing.

Seven (7) weeks are available for this exercise across the first part of the course and one extra week after semester break (Weeks 2, 3, 4 then 6, 7, 8 and Week 11). Each of the four ‘critical questions’ that students choose to do will be assessed as detailed in Assessment Criteria document (see Blackboard). Do only four.

Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site.

AI Use: This assessment task will be completed in-person. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy.

assessments.task_description:
Week 2-12 students assessed on active participation (not attendance) in seminars = 10%

Each seminar marked as follows (converted to 10)

Full marks: Readings covered and critically considered through participation in seminar discussion. Insightful questions raised for discussion, open and useful points of discussion, or clear engagement in others’ discussion (evidenced by making notes or other non-verbal cues).

Partial marks: Present in class but did not contribute to discussion, or did not so in an informed way (as above).

Zero marks: absent.

NB: If students are consistently unable to be in class (and have SAP, Med Certs/other justifiable absence) they may arrange to submit short summaries of readings to Blackboard for comment. This cannot be retroactive (i.e. must be arranged in advance) and must be arranged with the course coordinator.

assessments.task_description:
During the first class each student will choose one week to be responsible for leading the seminar discussion

Lead the seminar in class (ONCE – see schedule for “*student-led”): detail ONE work listed & raise 1-2 class discussion questions that show you have read all material.

Oral presentation (5-7 mins) + MUST provide notes in hard copy at beginning of the class.

Your notes for the discussion should show:

  • A very brief summary of key reading – what is the material essentially about (in 1-2 concise sentences)?
  • What is the author’s central argument, or the argument you find most compelling?
  • What key points from this reading assist us to consider a broader topic/concept?
  • What further questions are raised by the author/s for considering the topic/concept? (reference related literature)
  • Draft 1-2 questions designed to generate class discussion of the reading and topic.


Marking criteria and/or marking rubrics are available in the ‘Assessment’ folder in Blackboard for this course.

Students are assessed as follows:

Notes handed in at beginning of seminar; comprehension of the material, good summary of central argument and key points; a well drafted and considered question for class discussion; clearly spoken, keeping to time and engagement of other students throughout class time.

NOTE: IF A STUDENT IS UNWELL they may arrange to lead the seminar on an alternative day. They must be in touch before the class to notify the course coordinator and arrange an alternative.

AI Use: This assessment task evaluates student’s abilities, skills and knowledge to read and consider the literature. AI tools that summarise the literature may be used to generate key points, but students should be aware that these tools often miss the subtleties of argument, may misrepresent authors' ideas or not provide you with enough knowledge to devise good questions for discussion.

A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Students must complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub.

assessments.task_description:
2800 words: Self devised essay question.

Self devised research question, based on course material OR Students may focus on a topic they are passionate about and which they may wish to explore further as part of a focus of life, recreational interests, or future study (an Honours thesis?). The final essay asks you to devise your own critical question and then explore debates that inform that question using the conceptual or theoretical literature in anthropology. Students are encouraged to choose their topic early in the semester and read accordingly. In week 10 students declare their topic and outline the draft question. This is assessed (5%). Week 10 is also an opportunity to discuss your essay topic, planning and development and gain some feedback.

Marking criteria and/or marking rubrics are available in the ‘Assessment’ folder in Blackboard for this course.

AI Use: This assessment task evaluates student’s abilities, skills and knowledge to read and consider the literature. AI tools that summarise the literature may be used to generate key points, but students should be aware that these tools often miss the subtleties of argument, may misrepresent authors' ideas or not provide you with enough knowledge to devise good questions for an adequate critical analysis.

A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Students must complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub.

learning_activities.topic:
What is theory and how might anthropological theories prepare us for the future?

See Blackboard for weekly activity schedule.

Course overview and workshop: How to write a critical question arising from a summary. How to participate & ask discussion questions.

Each student will introduce themselves by identifying a topic of interest in anthropology and nominating a week for leading discussion. ALSO 1. Examine Tsing’s opening pages – what are we in for? 2. Raise questions about the history of anth. theory (Ortner). Consider what constitutes theory (Million’s) and ‘critique’.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
